questions.q: What prompted Gretchen Rubin to start exploring her senses?
a: A doctor's warning that she risked a detached retina
A friend who had lost their sense of smell
A mindfulness course she had agreed to teach
A visit to a perfume factory in France
questions.why: An eye checkup reminded her she was at risk for a detached retina, and the thought of losing her sight woke her up.

questions.q: What phone change does Rubin recommend to help you notice the real world?
a: Switching the screen to grayscale
Turning off every notification
Leaving the phone in another room
Deleting all social media apps
questions.why: In her list of sight practices, she says a gray screen makes the phone easier to put down so you can look around.

questions.q: Why does Rubin value the sense of smell so highly?
a: It anchors us in the present and can bring back the past
It helps us judge the quality of food and drink
It makes us more attractive to the people around us
It sharpens our memory for faces and names
questions.why: She says a well-trained nose keeps you grounded in the now, and that smell is the sense most able to transport you back.

questions.q: Which practice does Rubin suggest for training your nose?
a: Linger over smells like morning coffee to learn them
Avoid all strong scents for a month
Compare every new smell to a color
Eat meals with your nose pinched
questions.why: Her first smell exercise is to take a deep breath over the coffee mug and savor it, since regular smells become identifiable.

questions.q: What does Rubin mean by embodied cognition?
a: The whole body takes part in thinking and creativity
The mind learns best while sitting perfectly still
Emotions are stored only in the brain
Touch matters less than sight and hearing
questions.why: She defines it as the idea that the entire body is involved in thinking, suggesting you combine movement with learning.
